questions.q: Which component splits text into tokens and maps them to integer IDs?
questions.why: Models can't read letters - the tokenizer turns text into a list of numbers (token IDs) the model can work with.
questions.example: "unbelievable" might become  un | believ | able  ->  [403, 8812, 540].
questions.say: Models can't read letters. The tokenizer cuts text into pieces called tokens, and turns each one into a number the model can work with.

questions.q: Which method builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pairs of symbols?
questions.why: BPE starts from single characters and keeps gluing the most common pair together, so frequent words end up as one token.
questions.example: "l"+"o" -> "lo", then "lo"+"w" -> "low": common words become single tokens.
questions.say: It starts from single characters and keeps merging the most common pair, so frequent words end up as a single token.

questions.q: Which concept places tokens with similar meaning close together as vectors?
questions.why: Each token becomes a vector of numbers; tokens used in similar ways get vectors that point in similar directions.
questions.example: "cat" and "dog" sit close together, "cat" and "carburettor" far apart.
questions.say: Every token becomes a vector, a list of numbers. Words used in similar ways, like cat and dog, end up close together.

questions.q: Which concept tells the model the order of the tokens?
questions.why: Attention by itself ignores word order, so a position signal is added to every token vector.
questions.example: Without it, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical.
questions.say: Attention on its own ignores word order. Adding a position signal is what tells dog bites man apart from man bites dog.

questions.q: Which mechanism lets every token look at all other tokens of the same sequence?
questions.why: Every token builds a weighted mix of all the other tokens, so each word understands its context.
questions.example: In "the bank of the river", "bank" pays attention to "river" - not to money.
questions.say: Each token looks at all the other tokens and mixes in what is relevant. In the bank of the river, bank pays attention to river.

questions.q: Which technique stops the model from looking at future tokens?
questions.why: A mask hides later positions, so while learning to predict the next word the model can't peek at it.
questions.example: Like covering the rest of a sentence with your hand while guessing the next word.
questions.say: A mask hides the words that come later, so while learning to predict the next word, the model can't peek at it.

questions.q: Which idea runs several attention mechanisms in parallel, each learning a different relation?
questions.why: Several attention heads run side by side, and each can specialise in a different kind of relationship.
questions.example: One head tracks grammar (who did what), another tracks which word a pronoun refers to.
questions.say: Several attention heads run side by side. One might track grammar, another which word a pronoun refers to.

questions.q: Which problem made early encoder-decoder models forget long sentences?
questions.why: The old encoder squeezed the whole sentence into one fixed vector - long inputs simply didn't fit.
questions.example: Like summarising a whole book in one sentence, then translating only from that sentence.
questions.say: Old models squeezed a whole sentence into one fixed vector. For long sentences, important details simply got lost.

questions.q: Which architecture is the basis of modern large language models?
questions.why: Transformers use attention instead of step-by-step recurrence, so they train in parallel and scale to huge sizes.
questions.example: GPT, Llama, Claude and Gemini are all built from stacked Transformer blocks.
questions.say: It replaces step by step processing with attention, so it trains in parallel and scales to huge sizes. G P T and Llama are built on it.

questions.q: Which training stage predicts the next token on enormous amounts of text?
questions.why: In pretraining the model reads huge amounts of text and learns one thing: predict the next token.
questions.example: "The capital of France is ..." -> it learns to put high probability on "Paris".
questions.say: The model reads a huge amount of text and learns one simple task: predict the next token. Knowledge emerges from that.

questions.q: Which method trains a reward model from human preference rankings?
questions.why: Humans rank several answers, a reward model learns those preferences, and the LLM is then tuned to score high.
questions.example: People prefer the polite, correct reply, so the model learns to give replies like that.
questions.say: People rank several answers, a reward model learns what they prefer, and the language model is then tuned to score well.

questions.q: Which method learns directly from preference pairs, without a reward model?
questions.why: DPO skips the separate reward model: it pushes the chosen answer's probability up and the rejected one's down directly.
questions.example: Given (better answer, worse answer) pairs, it simply learns to prefer the better one.
questions.say: It skips the reward model. Given a better and a worse answer, it directly makes the better one more likely.

questions.q: Which setting sharpens or flattens the probabilities when choosing the next token?
questions.why: Scores are divided by the temperature before softmax: low = sharper and safer, high = flatter and more creative.
questions.example: T = 0.2 almost always picks the top word; T = 1.5 often picks surprising words.
questions.say: Low temperature makes the model pick the safest word. High temperature flattens the odds, so its choices get more creative.

questions.q: Which decoding method samples only among the k most likely tokens?
questions.why: Top-k throws away everything except the k most likely tokens, then samples only among those.
questions.example: With k = 3, only the 3 best next words can ever be chosen - no weird long-tail words.
questions.say: Only the k most likely tokens are kept, and the model samples among them. Strange, unlikely words are cut off.

questions.q: Which concept lets a model learn a task from examples in the prompt, without changing its weights?
questions.why: The examples in the prompt steer the answer while the model's weights stay exactly the same.
questions.example: Show "happy -> positive, awful -> negative", then "great -> ?" and it answers "positive".
questions.say: The examples in the prompt steer the answer, while the model's weights stay exactly the same.

questions.q: Which approach fetches relevant documents first and then lets the LLM answer from them?
questions.why: RAG first retrieves relevant documents, then gives them to the LLM so it can answer from real sources.
questions.example: Asking about your company handbook: the right pages are found first, then the model answers from them.
questions.say: First the relevant documents are retrieved, then the model answers from them. That keeps answers grounded in real sources.

questions.q: Which problem describes fluent but invented answers?
questions.why: The model is trained to sound fluent, not to be correct, so it can confidently invent facts.
questions.example: Citing a research paper with a real-sounding title that doesn't exist.
questions.say: The model is trained to sound fluent, not to be correct. So it can confidently invent facts, like a paper that doesn't exist.

questions.q: Which step splits documents into pieces that can be embedded and retrieved?
questions.why: Long documents are cut into small pieces so each piece can be embedded and retrieved on its own.
questions.example: A 300-page manual becomes ~1,000 chunks of a paragraph or two each.
questions.say: Long documents are cut into small pieces, so each piece can be embedded and found on its own.

questions.q: Which technique finds the nearest vectors quickly by trading a little accuracy for speed?
questions.why: Approximate Nearest Neighbour search skips checking every vector and accepts a tiny accuracy loss for huge speed.
questions.example: Finding the top 5 matches among 10 million vectors in milliseconds instead of seconds.
questions.say: Instead of checking every vector, it takes smart shortcuts. A tiny bit less accurate, but thousands of times faster.

questions.q: Which method merges several ranked result lists by summing 1 divided by (k plus rank)?
questions.why: RRF scores each document by summing 1 / (k + rank) across lists, so items ranked well everywhere rise to the top.
questions.example: Rank 1 in keyword search and rank 2 in vector search beats rank 1 in only one of them.
questions.say: Each document gets points from every ranked list, and more points for a higher rank. Documents ranked well everywhere win.
